svg.title: Figure 2 | Context, Tools and Orchestration
svg.desc: Check information, tools and orchestration: the correct requirements, executable capabilities, and retry, restore and stop conditions must work together.

g.font-family: Arial, Noto Sans CJK TC, sans-serif
g.text: Figure 2 | Context, Tools and Orchestration
1. Context: does the engineer have the right information?
Imagine an engineer assigned a repair but handed a
specification from three years ago that says “at most two
subjects on weekends.”
Following that specification would make the bug permanent.
Context gives the model the requirements, code, error messages
and test results needed for this task.
The goal is correct, relevant information from the right
version, rather than the largest possible pile of data.
2. Tools: does the engineer have the tools to work?
Suppose the engineer knows exactly where the bug is, but the
company only permits reading code and provides no way to
change files.
The engineer can explain how to fix it but cannot carry out
the repair.
Tools are the toolbox: reading and writing files, searching
code and running tests.
Being able to suggest a change does not establish the ability
to make that change.
3. Orchestration: who manages the order of work and stopping
conditions?
Suppose the engineer immediately changes more than ten files,
runs no tests and declares the job complete.
Orchestration is like a project manager: check the
specification, make the change and test it; on failure, decide
whether to retry, restore or stop.
When the AI chooses its next step, orchestration can still
control its tool calls and the scope of actions it may execute
Having tools and using them correctly are separate concerns.
Check information, tools and orchestration: the correct
requirements, executable capabilities, and retry, restore and
stop conditions must work together.
